A **diagonal** matrix is invertible exactly when none of its diagonal entries is zero, and
its inverse is obtained by **reciprocating each diagonal entry** — so it is diagonal too.
**Step 1 — write a general diagonal matrix.**
D = diag(d₁, d₂, …, dₙ)
**non-singular** means |D| = d₁d₂⋯dₙ ≠ 0, so **every dᵢ ≠ 0**.
**Step 2 — guess the inverse and verify.** Take
E = diag(1/d₁, 1/d₂, …, 1/dₙ)
which is well defined because no dᵢ is zero. Multiplying two diagonal matrices multiplies
their corresponding entries, so
DE = diag(d₁ × 1/d₁, …, dₙ × 1/dₙ) = diag(1, 1, …, 1) = **I** ✓
and ED = I likewise. So **D⁻¹ = E**, which is **diagonal** ✓
**A worked example.**
D = [[2, 0, 0], [0, 5, 0], [0, 0, −1]], with |D| = 2 × 5 × (−1) = −10 ≠ 0
D⁻¹ = [[1/2, 0, 0], [0, 1/5, 0], [0, 0, −1]]
and multiplying the two gives the identity ✓ The inverse is again diagonal.
**Why the other options fail.**
**scalar matrix** ✗ — a scalar matrix is kI, with all diagonal entries **equal**. The
inverse of diag(2, 5) is diag(1/2, 1/5), whose entries differ, so it is diagonal but not
scalar. (A scalar matrix's inverse *is* scalar, but the question asks about **any**
diagonal matrix.)
**skew-symmetric** ✗ — a skew-symmetric matrix has **zeros** on its diagonal, so a diagonal
matrix is skew-symmetric only if it is the zero matrix, which is singular and has no
inverse at all.
**zero matrix** ✗ — the zero matrix is singular, so it is excluded by "non-singular", and
in any case a product with it can never be I.
**The general principle.** Diagonal matrices are closed under addition, multiplication,
transposition and inversion — they behave like ordinary numbers, entry by entry, which is
why they are so convenient to compute with.
∴ diagonal matrix.

The **constant term** of the characteristic equation carries the determinant, and |adj A|
follows from it.
**Step 1 — recover |A| from the characteristic equation.** For a 3 × 3 matrix the
characteristic equation has the form
λ³ − (tr A)λ² + (sum of 2×2 principal minors)λ − |A| = 0
Comparing with the given
λ³ − 5λ² − 3λ + 2 = 0
the constant term is **+2**, and it equals −|A|:
−|A| = 2
**|A| = −2**
**Step 2 — apply the adjugate formula.** For a matrix of order n,
**|adj A| = |A|^(n−1)**
With n = 3:
|adj A| = |A|² = (−2)² = **4** ✓
**A second way to get |A|.** Every matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation
(Cayley–Hamilton), and substituting λ = 0 into det(λI − A) = 0 gives
det(−A) = (−1)³ det A = −|A|
while the polynomial at λ = 0 is **+2**. So −|A| = 2 and **|A| = −2** ✓ the same value.
**Why the sign does not matter here.** |adj A| = |A|², a **square**, so whichever sign
convention is used for the characteristic polynomial, |A| = ±2 and
|adj A| = 4 ✓ The answer is robust against the one thing most easily got wrong in this
topic.
**What else the equation tells us.** The coefficient of λ² gives the **trace**: tr A = 5.
And the three eigenvalues are the roots of λ³ − 5λ² − 3λ + 2 = 0, whose product is −2 =
|A| ✓ and whose sum is 5 = tr A ✓ — two consistency checks available for free.
**The distractors.** **25** is |A|² with |A| mistaken for 5, the trace rather than the
determinant — the likeliest confusion, since 5 is the number most visible in the equation.
**9** and **1/2** come from similar misreadings of which coefficient is which.
∴ 4.

The identity A² − B² = (A − B)(A + B) is **not** automatic for matrices, because matrix
multiplication does not commute. Expanding shows exactly what it requires.
**Step 1 — expand the right-hand side** carefully, keeping the order of every product:
(A − B)(A + B) = A(A + B) − B(A + B)
= A² + **AB** − **BA** − B²
**Step 2 — compare with the left-hand side.**
A² − B² = A² + AB − BA − B²
Cancelling A² and −B² from both sides,
0 = AB − BA
**AB = BA** ✓
So the identity holds **precisely when A and B commute** ✓
**Why the other options are wrong — each is sufficient but not necessary.**
**A = B** ✗ — certainly A commutes with itself, so the identity holds; but it is far too
strong a conclusion. Any commuting pair works, for instance A = I and B = any matrix.
**Either A or B is the zero matrix** ✗ — again sufficient (everything commutes with 0) but
not necessary.
**Either A or B is the identity matrix** ✗ — sufficient (I commutes with everything) but
not necessary.
The question asks what **will be true**, meaning what **must** follow, and only AB = BA
does.
**A counter-example showing commuting really is needed.** Take
A = [[1, 1], [0, 1]] and B = [[1, 0], [1, 1]]
AB = [[2, 1], [1, 1]] while BA = [[1, 1], [1, 2]], so **AB ≠ BA**. Then
A² − B² = [[1, 2], [0, 1]] − [[1, 0], [2, 1]] = [[0, 2], [−2, 0]]
(A − B)(A + B) = [[0, 1], [−1, 0]][[2, 1], [1, 2]] = [[1, 2], [−2, −1]]
The two differ ✗ exactly as the algebra predicts, since AB − BA ≠ 0.
**The wider lesson.** The familiar algebraic identities — (A + B)² = A² + 2AB + B² as well —
all hold for matrices **only** when the matrices commute. Writing out the expansion rather
than quoting the scalar identity is the safe habit.
∴ AB = BA.

A **binomial** situation: 11 independent steps, each forward with probability 0·4 or
backward with 0·6.
**Step 1 — express the position.** Let f be the number of forward steps, so the number of
backward steps is 11 − f, and the displacement is
f − (11 − f) = **2f − 11**
**Step 2 — impose "one step away from the start".** The distance from the start is
|2f − 11| = 1, so
2f − 11 = 1 ⟹ **f = 6**
or 2f − 11 = −1 ⟹ **f = 5**
Two cases, and they are mutually exclusive, so their probabilities add.
(Note that 2f − 11 is always **odd** for whole f, so after an odd number of steps the man
can never be at the start — he must be an odd distance away, and 1 is the nearest.)
**Step 3 — write the two binomial probabilities.**
P(f = 6) = ¹¹C₆ (0·4)⁶(0·6)⁵
P(f = 5) = ¹¹C₅ (0·4)⁵(0·6)⁶
**Step 4 — add, and simplify.** Note ¹¹C₆ = ¹¹C₅ = 462, so the common factor comes out:
P = ¹¹C₆ (0·4)⁵(0·6)⁵ [0·4 + 0·6]
= ¹¹C₆ (0·4 × 0·6)⁵ × 1
= **¹¹C₆ × (0·24)⁵** ✓
**Why the factorisation works.** Taking (0·4)⁵(0·6)⁵ out of both terms leaves 0·4 from the
first and 0·6 from the second, and those sum to exactly **1** — which is what collapses two
terms into one and produces the clean (0·24)⁵.
**A numerical check.** (0·24)⁵ ≈ 0·000796, and 462 × 0·000796 ≈ **0·368**. A probability of
about 37% of ending one step out is plausible for an 11-step walk biased backwards ✓
**The distractors.** **(0·48)⁵** uses 0·4 + 0·08 or doubles 0·24; **(0·12)⁵** halves it;
and ¹¹C₆ × (0·72)⁶ has both the wrong product and the wrong exponent. The key quantity is
the **product** 0·4 × 0·6 = 0·24, raised to the **fifth** power because five pairs of steps
are shared between the two cases.
∴ ¹¹C₆ × (0·24)⁵.

Independence is defined by P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B), and the key fact is that it **passes to
the complements**.
**Step 1 — start from the definition.** A and B are independent means
**P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B)**
**Step 2 — compute P(A′ ∩ B′).** By De Morgan, A′ ∩ B′ = (A ∪ B)′, so
P(A′ ∩ B′) = 1 − P(A ∪ B)
= 1 − [P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)]
= 1 − P(A) − P(B) + P(A)P(B) (using independence)
**Step 3 — factorise.**
= (1 − P(A)) − P(B)(1 − P(A))
= **(1 − P(A))(1 − P(B))** ✓
So independence of A and B is equivalent to
**P(A′ ∩ B′) = (1 − P(A))(1 − P(B))** ✓ which is the option given.
**Why the condition is equivalent, not merely implied.** Running the algebra backwards from
P(A′ ∩ B′) = (1 − P(A))(1 − P(B)) returns P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B), so the statement is a
genuine **criterion** for independence, which is what the question asks for.
**Why the other options fail.**
**A and B are mutually exclusive** ✗ — this is almost the **opposite** of independence. If
A ∩ B = ∅ then P(A ∩ B) = 0, and independence would then force P(A)P(B) = 0, meaning one of
them is impossible. Two events of positive probability cannot be both mutually exclusive
and independent — mutual exclusivity means knowing A occurred tells you B did **not**,
which is maximal dependence.
**P(A) = P(B)** ✗ — equal probabilities say nothing about how the events relate. A and A
itself have equal probabilities and are heavily dependent.
**P(A) + P(B) = 1** ✗ — again a statement about the individual probabilities alone, with no
bearing on their intersection.
The distinction the question tests is that independence is a condition on the
**intersection**, never on the individual probabilities.
∴ P(A′ ∩ B′) = (1 − P(A))(1 − P(B)).

This is **Bayes' theorem**: the child is known to be left-handed, and we must work backwards
to the probability that both parents were left-handed.
**Step 1 — write down the data.** The four parent combinations A, B, C, D are equally
likely, each with probability **1/4**, and the conditional chances of a left-handed child
are
P(L|A) = 0·24, P(L|B) = 0·09, P(L|C) = 0·17, P(L|D) = 0·22
**Step 2 — find P(L) by the law of total probability.**
P(L) = P(A)P(L|A) + P(B)P(L|B) + P(C)P(L|C) + P(D)P(L|D)
= (1/4)(0·24 + 0·09 + 0·17 + 0·22)
= (1/4)(**0·72**)
= **0·18**
**Step 3 — apply Bayes' theorem.**
P(A|L) = P(A)P(L|A) / P(L)
= [(1/4)(0·24)] / [(1/4)(0·72)]
**Step 4 — cancel the 1/4**, which appears in every term because the four cases are
equally likely:
= 0·24/0·72
= 24/72
= **1/3** ✓
**Why the 1/4 cancels.** When the prior probabilities are all equal, Bayes' theorem reduces
to comparing the **likelihoods** alone:
P(A|L) = 0·24 / (0·24 + 0·09 + 0·17 + 0·22)
So the answer is simply A's share of the total chance — a shortcut worth remembering
whenever the causes are equally likely.
**A sanity check on size.** Before learning the child is left-handed, P(A) = 1/4 = 0·25.
Learning that the child **is** left-handed should **raise** the chance that both parents
were left-handed, since that combination has the highest rate (24%). And indeed
1/3 ≈ 0·333 > 0·25 ✓ The evidence points the right way.
**The complete posterior**, for interest:
P(A|L) = 24/72 = **1/3**, P(B|L) = 9/72 = **1/8**, P(C|L) = 17/72, P(D|L) = 22/72 = 11/36
and these sum to 72/72 = **1** ✓

world population and plays **no part** in the calculation — a deliberate distraction, since
all the information needed is in the four conditional rates and the equal priors.
∴ 1/3.

**every** a in the set.
**Step 1 — write the condition.** With a ∗ b = a + b − ab,
a ∗ e = a + e − ae
and this must equal a:
a + e − ae = a
**Step 2 — solve for e.**
e − ae = 0
e(1 − a) = 0
**Step 3 — divide by (1 − a).** This is the step the question is built around: the set is
"all rationals **other than 1**", so a ≠ 1 and therefore **1 − a ≠ 0**. Dividing is legal,
and
**e = 0** ✓
**Step 4 — check the other side**, since ∗ must be checked both ways unless commutativity
is known:
e ∗ a = 0 + a − 0 × a = **a** ✓
(In fact a ∗ b = a + b − ab is symmetric in a and b, so ∗ is commutative and one check
would have sufficed.)
**Step 5 — check 0 belongs to the set.** Q₁ is the rationals excluding 1, and 0 ≠ 1, so
**0 ∈ Q₁** ✓ An identity outside the set would not count.
**Verifying with numbers.**
2 ∗ 0 = 2 + 0 − 0 = **2** ✓
(−3) ∗ 0 = −3 + 0 − 0 = **−3** ✓
(1/2) ∗ 0 = 1/2 ✓

operation is really ordinary multiplication in disguise, under the substitution

and removing it is exactly what makes (Q₁, ∗) a **group**, with identity a = 0 (that is
u = 1) and inverse a⁻¹ = a/(a − 1).

absorbing element, not an identity ✗ — and that is precisely why it had to be excluded.
∴ 0.

**Step 1 — differentiate.**
y = −x² + 6x − 3
**dy/dx = −2x + 6**
**Step 2 — solve dy/dx > 0.**

6 > 2x

**downward** and has a **maximum** at its vertex. Completing the square:
y = −(x² − 6x) − 3 = −(x − 3)² + 9 − 3 = **−(x − 3)² + 6**
so the vertex is at **(3, 6)** — the highest point of the curve.
A downward parabola **rises** to the left of its vertex and **falls** to the right, so it
is increasing exactly on **x < 3** ✓ which confirms the calculus.
**Checking with values.**
at x = 0: y = −3
at x = 2: y = −4 + 12 − 3 = **5**
at x = 3: y = −9 + 18 − 3 = **6** — the maximum
at x = 4: y = −16 + 24 − 3 = **5**
at x = 6: y = −36 + 36 − 3 = −3
Rising up to x = 3, falling afterwards ✓

**x > 3** ✗ — this is where the function **decreases**, the answer one would get from

direction. Writing −2x + 6 > 0 as 6 > 2x first, and only then dividing by the **positive**
2, avoids the issue altogether.
∴ x < 3.

**P = p ∧ ~q** and **Q = r**
**Step 2 — negate the consequent.**
~Q = **~r**
**Step 3 — negate the antecedent** using **De Morgan's law**, ~(A ∧ B) ≡ ~A ∨ ~B:
~P = ~(p ∧ ~q)
= ~p ∨ ~(~q)
= **~p ∨ q**
(the double negation on q collapsing to q — the step most easily missed.)
**Step 4 — assemble.**
inverse = ~P → ~Q = **(~p ∨ q) → (~r)** ✓

**r → p ∧ (~q)** ✗ — this is the plain **converse**, with no negations at all.
**(~p) ∨ (~q) → r** ✗ — here De Morgan has been misapplied: negating p ∧ ~q gave ~p ∨ ~q
instead of ~p ∨ q, and the consequent was left un-negated.

the question worth doing slowly.

**inverse:** negate both parts, keep the order
**De Morgan:** ~(A ∧ B) ≡ ~A ∨ ~B — the ∧ becomes ∨ when the negation goes inside
Applying the first without the second leaves the antecedent as ~(p ∧ ~q), which is correct
but not in any of the offered forms; pushing the negation inside is what produces ~p ∨ q.

says "if it is **not** the case that p holds and q does not — that is, if p fails **or** q
holds — then r does not". The "and" turning into "or" under negation is the content of De
Morgan's law.
∴ (~p) ∨ q → (~r).

jumps wildly, because every interval — however short — contains both rationals and

**irrationals**: f takes the value x at each, so those values tend to **a**.

continuous at 0** ✓

rational and an irrational. So no matter how small a neighbourhood of a is taken, it
contains points where f is 0 and points where f is near a. When a ≠ 0 those two values stay
a fixed distance apart and the function cannot settle — but when a = 0 they are both near
0, and the conflict disappears.

y = x, and those two lines **meet** at the origin. A function pinched between two curves
that touch is continuous at the point of contact, and nowhere else is it pinched at all.

**discontinuous everywhere** ✗ — it is continuous at 0, by step 2.
**continuous at all rational numbers** ✗ — take a = 1, rational: along irrationals near 1,
f(x) ≈ 1, but f(1) = 0, so it is discontinuous there.
∴ continuous only at x = 0.

The **coefficient of variation** expresses the standard deviation as a **percentage of the
mean**:
**CV = (σ / x̄) × 100**
**Step 1 — substitute what is given.** CV = 60 and σ = 21:
60 = (21/x̄) × 100
**Step 2 — rearrange.**
60 x̄ = 21 × 100
60 x̄ = 2100
**x̄ = 2100/60 = 35** ✓
**Check.** With mean 35 and standard deviation 21,
CV = (21/35) × 100 = 0·6 × 100 = **60** ✓ as required.
**What the answer means.** A coefficient of variation of 60% says the spread is more than
half the size of the average value — a fairly scattered distribution. And indeed σ = 21 is
large relative to x̄ = 35.
**Why CV is used at all.** The standard deviation alone cannot say whether a distribution
is widely spread, because it carries the **units** of the data: σ = 21 cm is huge for the
heights of a class but negligible for the distances between cities. Dividing by the mean
removes the units, so the CV is a **pure number** and two distributions measured in
different units can be compared directly.
**The three quantities, and which is which.**
**mean x̄** — the centre
**standard deviation σ** — the spread, in the data's own units
**CV = 100σ/x̄** — the spread **relative** to the centre, as a percentage
Rearranged, the formula gives any one from the other two: **x̄ = 100σ/CV** ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **21** is σ itself, offered for anyone who reads the question
too quickly; **60** is the CV, likewise; and **30** would follow from CV = 70 or from
σ = 18. Only 35 satisfies (21/x̄) × 100 = 60.
**A caution about the 100.** Leaving it out gives x̄ = 21/60 = 0·35, a hundredfold error.
The CV is quoted as a **percentage**, so the factor 100 is part of the definition, not a
decoration.
∴ 35.

The denominator x² − 1 tends to **0** as x → 1, yet the quotient tends to the finite number
π — and that can only happen if the **numerator tends to 0 as well**.
**Step 1 — state the principle.** Suppose
lim(x→1) N(x)/D(x) = L, finite, with lim(x→1) D(x) = 0
Then
lim N(x) = lim [N(x)/D(x) × D(x)] = L × 0 = **0**
using the product rule for limits, which applies because both factors have limits.
**Step 2 — apply it here.** With N(x) = f(x) − 2 and D(x) = x² − 1, and L = π:
lim(x→1) [f(x) − 2] = π × 0 = **0**
**Step 3 — conclude.**
lim(x→1) f(x) − 2 = 0
**lim(x→1) f(x) = 2** ✓
**A concrete function that fits.** Take f(x) = 2 + π(x² − 1). Then
[f(x) − 2]/(x² − 1) = π(x² − 1)/(x² − 1) = **π** for all x ≠ 1 ✓ the given condition
and lim(x→1) f(x) = 2 + π(0) = **2** ✓
**Why the value π is irrelevant.** Any finite limit L would give the same conclusion: the
numerator must vanish. The examiner has chosen π precisely because it looks as though it
ought to appear in the answer, and it does not. Options (2) and (3), 3 and 1, are likewise
unrelated to it — the only number that matters is the **2** subtracted in the numerator.
**What would happen otherwise.** If lim f(x) were, say, 5, then the numerator would tend
to **3** while the denominator tends to 0, and the quotient would be unbounded — no finite
limit, let alone π. So the condition in the question forces the numerator's limit.
**The general pattern.** Whenever a question says "the limit of a quotient is finite" and
the denominator plainly vanishes, the first deduction is always that the **numerator
vanishes too**. That single observation answers a whole family of problems, including the
standard "find a and b so that the limit exists" type.
∴ 2.
